chief_complaint: wheezing, runny nose, and tachypnea in infant
hpi_details: A 1-year-old male is brought to the clinic with wheezing, rhinorrhea, and tachypnea. His parent reports that symptoms began recently and have gradually worsened.
ideas: The parent thinks the baby caught a severe chest cold or a bad viral bug from other children at daycare.
concerns: parent is worried about breathing difficulty and dehydration
expectations: parent wants an evaluation and guidance on supportive care
social_hx: Lives with parents; no tobacco-smoke exposure reported

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pediatric Bronchiolitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Pediatric Bronchiolitis: Supportive care, hydration, nasal suctioning, avoid albuterol, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: wheezing, runny nose, and tachypnea in infant
Key HPI features: A 1-year-old male is brought to the clinic with wheezing, rhinorrhea, and tachypnea. His parent reports that symptoms began recently and have gradually worsened.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Pediatric Bronchiolitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that wheeze in an infant should be managed as asthma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Using bronchodilators, corticosteroids, or antibiotics routinely in uncomplicated bronchiolitis.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as apnea, cyanosis, severe respiratory distress, or poor feeding.
management_principles: Assess oxygenation, work of breathing, hydration, and risk factors such as prematurity or cardiopulmonary disease.
Provide clinician-directed supportive care; bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics are not routine for uncomplicated bronchiolitis.
Send the child for emergency evaluation for apnea, cyanosis, severe work of breathing, exhaustion, poor feeding, or signs of dehydration.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A viral lower respiratory tract infection in infants causing rhinorrhea, cough, wheeze, tachypnea, and increased work of breathing.
red_flags: Severe respiratory distress or poor feeding with dehydration

must_ask.say: How much is your baby feeding, and how many wet diapers have they had today?
Have you noticed pauses in breathing, blue lips, chest retractions, or nasal flaring?
When did the runny nose and cough begin, and has the breathing become faster or more difficult?
Was your baby born prematurely or do they have heart, lung, or immune problems?
Has your baby been around anyone with a cold, or exposed to cigarette smoke?

history.answer: He has been wheezing and breathing fast since yesterday, and his nose has been running for a few days.
It began 3 days ago with a clear runny nose and mild warmth, but over the last 2 days his cough worsened and his breathing became faster and noisier.
He breathes fast even while resting in my lap, and I can see his chest pulling in a little underneath his ribs.
His fast breathing and wheezing have been constant since yesterday, not coming and going in sudden spells.
No, this is the very first time he has ever had fast breathing or wheezing.
He has trouble sleeping flat because his nose gets blocked and his cough wakes him up, so he sleeps better propped on my chest.
Crying and trying to nurse make him breathe much faster, while sitting upright and using a cool humidifier seemed to help a tiny bit.
Yes, I hear a high-pitched musical whistling sound every time he breathes out.
He has a frequent wet cough, and he seems to swallow the clear mucus after coughing.
He had a low fever around 38 degrees Celsius two days ago, but no severe shivering or high spikes today.
He is too young to speak, but he becomes fussy and irritable during coughing fits.
He is fussier than usual, but he still makes eye contact, smiles at his toys, and is not unusually sleepy or limp.
No, there was no sudden choking, gagging, or coughing while eating or playing with small toys.
No, he has never paused his breathing, turned blue around his lips, or had pale spells.
He drinks only about half of his usual formula bottles because he stops to breathe, and his wet diapers dropped from six down to three or four today.
No, his legs and ankles are not swollen at all, and his weight has been stable.
No, he does not look pale, and there has been no blood in his stool, vomit, or saliva.
No, he has never had any heart murmurs, asthma, or previous chest infections.
No, he has never used an inhaler, spacer, or breathing machine before.
No, we have not given him aspirin, ibuprofen, or any cold medicines that could affect his breathing.
No, neither my spouse nor I smoke, and nobody smokes inside or around our home.
He goes to a small daycare twice a week, and two other babies in his infant room had colds with runny noses this week.
He was born full-term at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery without complications, weighing 3.2 kilograms, and had no NICU stay.
His growth has followed the normal percentiles, and all of his routine childhood vaccinations are completely up to date.
He has been very healthy and has never had surgery, hospitalizations, or serious illnesses before.
He does not take any regular prescription medications; we gave him a single dose of infant acetaminophen two days ago for the fever.
He has no known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
There is no family history of asthma, allergies, eczema, or lung diseases in childhood.
He lives in an apartment with both parents, and we have no pets or indoor mold.
I thought he might have caught a really bad chest cold from the other toddlers at his daycare.
I am terrified that his breathing will get worse or that he will get severely dehydrated since he is drinking less milk.
I want you to check his lungs, tell us if he is getting enough oxygen, and guide us on how to take care of him safely.

exam.finding: Temperature 37.8°C, heart rate 128 beats/min, respiratory rate 48 breaths/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air.
Alert 1-year-old infant in mild respiratory distress with noticeable tachypnea and mild subcostal retractions, but no cyanosis or lethargy.
Bilateral clear anterior rhinorrhea; pharynx is mildly erythematous without tonsillar enlargement or exudate.
Bilateral tympanic membranes are pearly gray and translucent, without erythema, bulging, or effusion.
No cervical lymphadenopathy palpable; neck is supple with full passive range of motion.
Mild intercostal and subcostal retractions visible during inspiration; symmetric chest wall motion without localized tenderness.
Bilateral lung fields are resonant to percussion without areas of dullness.
Diffuse bilateral expiratory wheezing and scattered fine end-inspiratory crackles; no localized bronchial breath sounds.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs heard.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender; liver edge is palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin with smooth edge and no splenomegaly.
No pretibial or pedal edema bilaterally; capillary refill is under 2 seconds.
Skin turgor is preserved with normal skin recoil; oral mucosa is slightly tacky without skin rashes.
